summary: Reports a family of algorithms for retrieving large tables of management data with SNMP more efficiently than asking for one item at a time. It is an Experimental document that shares the ideas and invites discussion rather than defining a standard.

plainLanguage.summary: Instead of asking a librarian for one book at a time, you ask for a whole shelf at once. This explores ways to do that for network gadgets.

questions: how to retrieve large tables with snmp
what is snmp bulk table retrieval
how to retrieve snmp tables efficiently
how does get-next improve snmp retrieval
subtitle: Algorithms for efficiently retrieving large data tables from network devices via SNMP.

tldr.problem: Retrieving large tables of network management data using SNMP one row at a time requires O(rows × columns) operations, which is slow. Simply asking for whole rows reduces this to O(rows), but serial operations are still time-consuming.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC describes two algorithms that use pipelining and parallelism to keep multiple SNMP requests in flight simultaneously. The pipelined algorithm uses multiple threads that each fetch different portions of the table. The parallel algorithm combines multiple threads into single requests, further reducing network traffic.
tldr.outcome: Prototype experiments show the pipelined algorithm achieves 121 entries per second versus 56 for serial retrieval, and the parallel algorithm reaches 320 entries per second—a 571% improvement over the serial baseline.

facts.label: Serial algorithm performance
facts.value: 56 entries per second on same table

facts.label: Parallel algorithm performance
facts.value: 320 entries per second on same table

today: RFC 1187 is an Experimental protocol that explores optimization techniques for SNMP rather than defining a standard. The algorithms it describes influenced later SNMP implementations and management practices for efficient bulk data retrieval.

sections.title: The Challenge of Bulk Table Retrieval
sections.content:
SNMP's get-next operator is powerful for table traversal but retrieving entire tables one row at a time is inefficient. The naive approach requires O(rows × columns) operations. For example, to fetch a routing table with 100 rows and 10 columns requires 1000 individual requests.

A better approach uses get-next to retrieve an entire row in a single operation, reducing the requirement to O(rows) operations. However, some argued this was still a weakness of SNMP. What was overlooked is that nothing prevents a management station from sending multiple get-next requests in parallel, achieving both pipelining and parallelism without changing the SNMP protocol or burdening the agent.
sections.plainLanguage: Network devices keep data organized like tables. SNMP is the tool to read them. The question is: can you read faster if you ask for multiple pieces at once instead of one at a time?

sections.title: Pipelining and Parallelism Concepts
sections.content:
The pipelined algorithm uses a multi-threaded approach where each thread generates its own stream of get-next requests for different rows in the table. The key insight is keeping several transactions in transit simultaneously, while both the agent and management station process transactions in parallel.

The algorithm adapts dynamically to network conditions and device loads by varying both the number of active threads and the retransmission timeout based on round-trip time and packet loss. Too few threads underutilize the connection; too many threads risk overrunning the agent. The ideal number is just enough so the next request arrives as the device finishes processing the previous one.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of waiting for one answer before asking the next question, ask multiple questions at once. But not so many that you overwhelm the device.

sections.title: Pipelined Algorithm Implementation
sections.content:
The pipelined algorithm starts with three threads covering different portions of the table. Each thread has associated state: the current request ID, the last message sent and retransmission count, the range of object instances for that thread, and the number of active threads when last sent.

The main loop waits for responses from any thread. When a response arrives, the algorithm checks if the returned object is beyond the thread's assigned range (meaning that portion is complete). If not, it stores the results and may create new threads to subdivide remaining ranges using an OID median function. The algorithm continues issuing new get-next requests for each active thread. Timeout values are dynamically adjusted based on round-trip time measurements, doubling on timeout and averaging with observed round-trip times during normal operation.
sections.plainLanguage: The algorithm divides the table into regions, asks about each region in parallel, and keeps adjusting how many regions to work on based on how fast it is getting answers.

sections.title: Parallel Algorithm and Performance
sections.content:
The parallel algorithm extends the pipelined approach by mapping multiple threads onto single SNMP operations. First, one thread retrieves instance identifiers by traversing a single column. Then, additional columns are retrieved using regular get operations (not get-next) since the identifiers are now known. The management station dynamically determines how many variables fit in a single request to minimize the total number of messages.

This two-step process is more efficient because agent execution of get is typically less expensive than get-next. On test tables of approximately 2500 entries, the pipelined algorithm achieved 121 entries per second while the parallel algorithm reached 320 entries per second.
sections.plainLanguage: First, find out how many rows the table has. Then, fetch the rest of the data in big batches instead of one column at a time.

sections.title: Practical Considerations
sections.content:
The specification includes several practical implementation details. Finding the median between two object identifiers is non-trivial because the OID space is neither uniform nor continuous. The algorithm makes a best-effort attempt by scanning sub-identifiers until a difference is found, then computing appropriate intermediate values.

The prototype found that many agent implementations incorrectly handle get-next requests with arbitrarily-generated suffixes, sometimes returning results lexicographically less than the request operand. This happens when instance identifiers use encoded addresses and agents compare only the least significant octet. The algorithm handles this by marking threads as dead and continuing, noting a possible gap in the table.
sections.plainLanguage: Real network devices sometimes have bugs. A good algorithm needs to detect these problems and work around them.

references.text: Case, J., Fedor, M., Schoffstall, M., and J. Davin, "Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP)", RFC 1157, May 1990.
